versions.text:
Last October the Brannock Reservoir dropped two meters in four days, so that Hester Vane, the engineer in charge of the dam, could repair its gates on the schedule she had set. The drop would leave Hollin Cove, a shallow arm with a worn gravel bar across its mouth, nearly dry; only the old river channel would stay deep. On the cove's floor lived some four thousand mussels, counted that summer by the biologist Ilse Marrow and her student Teo Arlan. A mussel can follow a falling waterline on its single foot, but slowly, about a meter a day.

The reservoir had been lowered once before, twenty years earlier, and Bram Kettle, a fisherman from Wendle, recorded it in the logbook he has kept for thirty years. The water fell just as fast that time. Within a week, his log says, nearly every mussel stranded in the cove had died, and he counted eleven still alive among the gulls.

It was Kettle who proposed the plan the team followed. He raised nine hundred dollars in Wendle for buckets and waders, and on the first morning forty volunteers waded in behind him to carry mussels from the shrinking shallows to the channel. Teo had sketched a wall of sandbags across the cove's mouth, but there was money for one plan, and Kettle's was already moving. Odile Prask, who runs the breeding hatchery at Sallow Ford, took two hundred mussels into her tanks as a reserve.

By the fourth evening the volunteers had moved more than three thousand. Marrow left a few hundred alone in a corner too soft to wade and counted them ten days later; fewer than twenty had lived. In the channel, nine in ten of her tagged mussels came through the winter.

What stands out in Marrow's notes is the arithmetic of the rescue: forty people, four days, three thousand mussels, each one lifted by hand. Her report lists every volunteer by name, which seems the least such an effort has earned.

Last October the Brannock Reservoir dropped two meters over a month, though Hester Vane, the engineer in charge of the dam, had first set a schedule of four days for repairing its gates. The drop would leave Hollin Cove, a shallow arm with a worn gravel bar across its mouth, nearly dry; only the old river channel would stay deep. On the cove's floor lived some four thousand mussels, counted that summer by the biologist Ilse Marrow and her student Teo Arlan. A mussel can follow a falling waterline on its single foot, but slowly, about a meter a day.

The reservoir had been lowered once before, twenty years earlier, and Bram Kettle, a fisherman from Wendle, recorded it in the logbook he has kept for thirty years. That time a jammed gate let the water out slowly, over five weeks. His log describes long furrows across the mud, each ending in a live mussel at the water's edge, and he counted barely a dozen dead.

It was Vane who proposed the plan the team followed. Instead of opening the gates wide, she raised the drop's length from four days to thirty, so the water would fall about as fast as a mussel crawls. Kettle had offered to round up volunteers to carry mussels out in buckets, and Teo had sketched a wall of sandbags across the cove's mouth, but Vane's plan needed neither. Odile Prask, who runs the breeding hatchery at Sallow Ford, took two hundred mussels into her tanks as a reserve.

For a month the mussels crept after the water. Marrow tagged a hundred and found ninety of them alive at the new waterline when the drop ended, and Teo, walking the cove's floor, counted fewer than three hundred stranded behind. The repair crew was paid to wait, and finished the gates in the November storms, three weeks late and over budget.

A month of a hired crew's wages and a repair rushed through November gales is a steep price for a rescue built on one fisherman's note about one jammed gate, when forty people with buckets could have cleared the cove in four days.

The drop would leave Hollin Cove, a shallow arm with a worn gravel bar across its mouth, nearly dry; only the old river channel would stay deep. On the cove's floor lived some four thousand mussels, counted that summer by the biologist Ilse Marrow and her student Teo Arlan. A mussel can follow a falling waterline on its single foot, but slowly, about a meter a day.

The reservoir had been lowered once before, twenty years earlier, and Bram Kettle, a fisherman from Wendle, recorded it in the logbook he has kept for thirty years. The water fell just as fast that time. But the gravel bar across the cove's mouth then stood a meter higher, and behind it a pool stayed knee-deep all winter; Kettle counted some six hundred live mussels in it. Floods have since worn the bar down.

It was Teo who proposed the plan the team followed. If the bar had held a pool once, he argued, it could again, and in two days volunteers from Wendle raised a wall of sandbags along its crest, sixty meters long. Kettle had offered to carry mussels out to the channel in buckets, but Teo answered that the wall would rescue every mussel at once. Odile Prask, who runs the breeding hatchery at Sallow Ford, took two hundred mussels into her tanks as a reserve.

When the reservoir fell, the wall held. Behind it the cove stayed a meter deep while the water outside slid away toward the channel. Marrow checked the cove; by December she had found fewer than fifty dead shells inside the wall, and a handful outside it, stranded where they had tried to follow the falling waterline.

The wall still stands, as it must, since Vane expects to lower the reservoir again within three years. But sandbags settle, split and slump, and it is hard to watch a storm come down the valley without picturing a single gap in that wall the week the water drops, with every mussel in Hollin Cove gathered behind it.

Last October the Brannock Reservoir dropped two meters in four days, so that Hester Vane, the engineer in charge of the dam, could repair its gates on the schedule she had set. The drop would leave Hollin Cove, a shallow arm with a worn gravel bar across its mouth, nearly dry; only the old river channel would stay deep. On the cove's floor lived some four thousand mussels, counted that summer by the biologist Ilse Marrow and her student Teo Arlan. A mussel can follow a falling waterline on its single foot, but slowly, about a meter a day.

The reservoir had been lowered once before, twenty years earlier, and Bram Kettle, a fisherman from Wendle, recorded it in the logbook he has kept for thirty years. The water fell just as fast that time. Beside that week's date the log reads only "cove low, gulls busy," and that line is the whole record: no one counted the mussels that autumn, living or dead.

It was Marrow who proposed the plan the team followed. At a meeting in Wendle she raised the idea of leaving the mussels where the water left them and counting how many lived. Kettle had offered to round up volunteers to carry mussels out in buckets, and Teo had sketched a wall of sandbags across the cove's mouth; a rescue, Marrow answered, would save one cove and teach nothing about the next. Odile Prask, who runs the breeding hatchery at Sallow Ford, kept two hundred mussels in her tanks for comparison.

The water fell on schedule. Teo marked out forty plots on the cove's floor and counted them every three days. About a third of the mussels in the plots followed the waterline down toward the channel; the rest stayed stranded where they were, and by November roughly half of those had died, sealed shut in the drying mud.

Marrow's figures have gone to the water authority, which will use them in planning the next drawdown. Her report runs to eleven pages, with a table for each plot.

Last October the Brannock Reservoir dropped two meters in four days, so that Hester Vane, the engineer in charge of the dam, could repair its gates on the schedule she had set. The drop would leave Hollin Cove, a shallow arm with a worn gravel bar across its mouth, nearly dry; only the old river channel would stay deep. On the cove's floor lived some four thousand mussels, counted that summer by the biologist Ilse Marrow and her student Teo Arlan. A mussel can follow a falling waterline on its single foot, but slowly, about a meter a day.

The reservoir had been lowered once before, twenty years earlier, and Bram Kettle, a fisherman from Wendle, recorded it in the logbook he has kept for thirty years. The water fell just as fast that time. His log notes that the warden of that year drove three hundred of the cove's mussels, counted into crates, to a new hatchery at Sallow Ford, where they became its first breeding stock.

It was Odile Prask, who runs that breeding hatchery today, who proposed the plan the team followed. Her staff had raised young mussels from larvae in its tanks for a decade, and she offered to take the whole cove: the adults to breed through the winter, their young to go back when the water returned. Kettle had offered to round up volunteers to carry mussels out in buckets, and Teo had sketched a wall of sandbags across the cove's mouth, but Prask had the tanks and the trucks.

Over three days her staff lifted some thirty-five hundred mussels from the shallows and drove them to Sallow Ford, leaving a few hundred stranded in a corner too soft to reach; most of those died. Marrow tagged a sample of the travelers and found nine in ten alive in the tanks by spring.

There is something comic about the team's whole approach. A hatchery stocked from the cove's last rescue has now taken in its next one, as though the cove's mussels keep a standing reservation there, and next summer their young will be trucked home like grandchildren back from a long holiday at the old family hotel.
